Professional Practice
Patient Safety & Infection Control
Introduction & Hospital Acquired Infection

This lesson introduces the foundations of infection control and patient safety, focusing on how healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) arise and spread within healthcare settings. It covers the chain of infection and its six links, the global burden and commonest clinical types of HAIs, and the two categories of precautions — standard and transmission-based — used to interrupt spread. The bulk of the lesson works through each of the eleven elements of standard precautions in turn: risk assessment, hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene, patient placement, personal protective equipment, aseptic technique, safe injection and sharps practices, environmental cleaning, linen handling, waste management, and reprocessing of reusable items. Together these form the everyday practices every healthcare worker relies on to protect patients, staff, and visitors.

Introduction to Infection Control

Infection control refers to the policies and procedures implemented to control and minimize the dissemination of infections in hospitals and other healthcare settings, with the main purpose of reducing infection rates.

Infection control was established as a formal entity in the early 1950s in the United States. By the late 1950s and 1960s, a small number of hospitals began to recognize healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and implement some infection control concepts. Early programs focused on surveillance for HAIs, incorporating basic epidemiology to identify risk factors. However, most were organized and managed by large academic centers rather than public health agencies, leading to sporadic efficiency and suboptimal outcomes.

The new era of infection control began through three pivotal events:

1. The Institute of Medicine's 1999 report on errors in health care
2. The 2002 Chicago Tribune reporting on HAIs
3. The 2004/2006 publications showing significant reductions in bloodstream infection rates through standardization of the central venous catheter insertion process

This new era is marked by consumer demand for transparency and accountability, increasing regulation, and expectations for rapid reductions in HAI rates.

The role of infection control is to prevent and reduce the risk of hospital-acquired infections. This is achieved through infection control programs in the forms of surveillance, isolation, outbreak management, environmental hygiene, employee health, education, and infection prevention policies and management.

Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAI)

Healthcare-associated infections (HAI) are defined as infections occurring in patients undergoing care in a healthcare facility which were not present or incubating at the time of admission. HAI also includes occupational infections in staff. Previous terms include “nosocomial” and “hospital-acquired” infection, but with healthcare delivery now taking place in many other settings, the term “healthcare-associated” infection is preferred.

In low- and middle-income countries, the burden of HAIs is high, varying between 5.7% and 19.2%. According to WHO data, the HAI rate is 25% in developing countries and 5–15% in developed countries. Vulnerable patients, such as those in intensive care units and those with invasive devices, are at higher risk of developing HAIs, contributing to increased morbidity, mortality, length of stay, and healthcare costs.

Every person who works at or visits a healthcare facility — including administrators, staff, patients, and carers — has a role and responsibility in preventing and controlling infection.

The Chain of Infection

Microorganisms are found in air, soil, water, and our bodies; some are helpful, others harmful. For an infection to spread, all steps in the chain of infection must occur. It is defined as: “the process that occurs when an infectious agent leaves its source or reservoir through a portal of exit and uses a mode of transmission to reach the portal of entry of a susceptible host.” The key to stopping the spread of infection is to break at least one link in the chain.

LinkDefinition & examples
Infectious AgentAn organism that can be transmitted and cause disease — e.g. viruses, bacteria, and parasites.
ReservoirWhere an infectious agent lives, grows, and multiplies — a person (patient or HCP) or the healthcare environment (dry surfaces such as bed rails and equipment; wet surfaces such as sinks and ventilators; medical devices such as catheters and IV lines).
Portal of ExitWhere an infectious agent leaves the reservoir — breaks in the skin, mucous membranes (eyes, nose, mouth), hands, blood, GI/urinary tracts (feces, vomit, urine), splashes from emesis, or an exposed needle in an open sharps container.
Mode of TransmissionHow an agent is directly or indirectly spread. Direct: skin-to-skin contact/kissing, or respiratory droplets (coughing, sneezing, talking, breathing). Indirect: through an extra step — suspended air particles (airborne), inanimate objects (vehicleborne), or arthropods (vectorborne).
Portal of EntryWhere an infectious agent enters a host — IV catheters and other devices, surgical incisions, mucous membranes, or breaks in the skin such as a sharp injury puncture.
Susceptible HostA host that an agent can enter and cause disease in — patients or healthcare workers. Susceptibility is increased by underlying conditions (diabetes, cancer, organ transplantation) that weaken immunity, certain medications (antibiotics, steroids, some chemotherapy), and medical devices/procedures (urinary catheters, tubes, surgery) that create additional entry routes.

Common Clinical Types of HAI

TypeKey featuresCommonest organisms
Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)Particularly catheter-associated (CAUTI); may affect bladder and/or kidneys.E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Proteus
Surgical Site Infection (SSI)Theater- or ward-origin; superficial (skin) or involving deeper tissues, organs, or implants.S. aureus (esp. MRSA), coagulase-negative staphylococci, vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE), Candida
Respiratory Tract InfectionsOf particular interest: ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) — a lung infection developing in a ventilated patient.S. aureus (MRSA), Gram-negative bacilli
Blood Stream InfectionsBacteraemia/septicaemia; may occur via IV drug delivery, surgery, or an infected skin ulcer.S. aureus, Enterococci, Bacteroides, Gram-negative bacilli, Candida
Gastrointestinal Tract InfectionsCauses pseudomembranous colitis.Clostridium difficile

Infection Prevention and Control (IPC)

The incidence of HAI can be reduced considerably by good infection prevention and control (IPC) practices. IPC is a “series of procedures and guidelines to prevent and control HAI and should be applied in all settings where healthcare is provided.” Unfortunately, IPC practices in the developing world are often below required standards, attributed to lack of resources, poorly designed and overcrowded settings, lack of basic facilities such as electricity and water, and chronic understaffing. While some IPC strategies are expensive, many approaches — such as hand hygiene and staff education and training — are low-cost and highly effective.

Two types of precautions are used to prevent and control infection in health care:

  • Standard precautions — covered in detail below.
  • Transmission-based precautions — interrupt the specific means of transmission of a particular infectious agent, and are used in addition to standard precautions. Understanding the means of transmission is important for deciding the most appropriate precautions to use. There are three categories: Contact precautions, Droplet precautions, and Airborne precautions.

Standard Precautions

Standard precautions are the minimum infection prevention and control practices that apply to all patient care, followed to reduce HAI transmission in any setting where healthcare is delivered. They should be used by ALL staff, in ALL care settings, at ALL times, for ALL patients — whether infection is known to be present or not — to ensure the safety of patients, staff, and visitors.

Standard precautions apply to blood, all body fluids (including CSF, pleural, peritoneal, and amniotic fluid), secretions (nasal secretions, sputum, tears, saliva), and excretions (feces, urine, and vomitus — except sweat), as well as non-intact skin and mucous membranes. Education and training are critical because they help healthcare workers make appropriate decisions and comply with recommended practices.

The 11 Elements of Standard Precautions

  1. Risk assessment
  2. Hand hygiene
  3. Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette
  4. Patient placement
  5. Personal protective equipment
  6. Aseptic technique
  7. Safe injections and sharps injury prevention
  8. Environmental cleaning
  9. Handling of laundry and linen
  10. Waste management
  11. Decontamination and reprocessing of reusable patient care items and equipment

1. Risk Assessment

Patients must be assessed for infection risk immediately on arrival at the care area (inpatient/outpatient/care home) — if possible before accepting a patient from another care area — and continuously reviewed throughout their stay. This assessment influences placement decisions in accordance with clinical/care needs.

Before any patient interaction, health workers should ask themselves whether they need protection because:

  • there is a risk of exposure to blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, splashes, and/or sprays;
  • the patient has symptoms of an undiagnosed infection (e.g. fever, cough, diarrhea) requiring transmission-based precautions; or
  • the patient has a known infection requiring transmission-based precautions.

2. Hand Hygiene

Hand hygiene is considered one of the most important ways to reduce the transmission of infectious agents that cause HAIs. It is a general term referring to any action of hand cleansing, including washing hands with soap and water, or applying an alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR — liquids, gels, and foams) to the surface of the hands.

The 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene

MomentWhen
1. Before touching a patientOn entering the patient zone before touching the patient.
2. Before a procedureImmediately before a procedure. Once hand hygiene is performed, the patient's environment should not be touched before the procedure.
3. After a procedure or body fluid exposure riskImmediately after a procedure or body fluid exposure (hands may be contaminated).
4. After touching a patientBefore leaving the patient zone.
5. After touching a patient's surroundingsEven when the patient has not been touched. Always perform hand hygiene before leaving the patient's room.

Hand Hygiene Technique

Nails must be clean and short; artificial nails, jewelry, and wristwatches should not be worn.

  • Handwashing with soap and water: wet hands and apply enough soap to cover all surfaces; vigorously rub all surfaces systematically, especially fingertips, thumbs, and finger webs; rinse with clean running water and dry thoroughly with a single-use towel. Total duration: 40–60 seconds. Leave single-use towels beside sinks, use a foot-operated bin to discard them, and use a towel to turn off the tap.
  • Alcohol-based handrub: apply 2–3 ml and rub hands until dry, systematically covering all surfaces. Total duration: 20–30 seconds.

Gloves do not replace the need for hand hygiene. Hand hygiene is required before putting on gloves and immediately after removing them. Hand hygiene products should not be applied to gloves.

3. Respiratory Hygiene and Cough Etiquette

Designed to minimize the risk of cross-transmission of known or suspected respiratory pathogens:

  • Cover the nose and mouth with a disposable tissue when sneezing, coughing, wiping, or blowing the nose; if unavailable, use the crook of the arm.
  • Dispose of all used tissues promptly into a waste bin.
  • Wash hands with soap and warm water after coughing, sneezing, using tissues, or contact with respiratory secretions or contaminated objects.
  • Where running water or hand hygiene facilities are lacking, use hand wipes followed by alcohol-based hand rub, and wash hands at the first available opportunity.
  • Keep contaminated hands away from the eyes, nose, and mouth.

4. Patient Placement

Single rooms have been shown to lower HAIs. When single rooms are limited, priority should go to patients with conditions that facilitate transmission of infectious material (e.g. draining wounds, stool incontinence, uncontained secretions), as well as patients at increased risk of acquiring HAIs or of adverse outcomes from them (e.g. immunosuppression, open wounds, indwelling catheters).

5. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

Health workers should select PPE based on risk assessment, remove and discard PPE when leaving the patient's room followed by hand hygiene, and discard/replace PPE if it becomes damaged, soiled, or wet. PPE includes gloves, gowns, medical masks, respirators, and eye protection.

a) Gloves

Worn during activities that may involve exposure to blood/body fluids, during contact precautions, and in outbreak situations. Remove gloves after caring for a patient — the same pair should never be worn for more than one patient — and change gloves between tasks if moving from a contaminated body site to another site on the same patient. Wearing gloves is not a substitute for hand hygiene. Sterile gloves are worn for aseptic procedures such as surgery or catheter insertion, and gloves must never be reused after reprocessing or decontamination.

b) Gown

Worn to protect skin and prevent soiling of clothing during activities likely to generate splashes or sprays of blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions. A waterproof apron should be worn over the gown if the gown is not fluid-resistant, or if splashing/spraying is anticipated. The soiled gown should be removed as soon as possible, followed by hand hygiene.

c) Medical Masks

Worn to protect the mucous membranes of the nose and mouth against splashes or sprays of body fluids, respiratory secretions, and chemicals, and to protect the patient during aseptic procedures (e.g. surgery or lumbar puncture).

d) Respirators

Worn (e.g. N95, FFP2) for protection from inhalation of airborne particles and/or when performing aerosol-generating procedures. A fit test should be done before first use, and a seal check performed every time a respirator is used. Replace the mask or respirator if damaged, soiled, or wet, or if breathing becomes difficult.

e) Eye Protection

Eye protection (visor or goggles) or a face shield is worn to protect the mucous membranes of the eyes during activities likely to generate splashes or sprays. Goggles should fit over and around the eyes or personal prescription lenses; a face shield should cover the forehead, extend below the chin, and wrap around the side of the face (more comfortable when worn with eyeglasses).

6. Aseptic Technique

Health workers should use sterile items and equipment for all aseptic procedures, and aseptic techniques for the insertion and maintenance of all invasive devices, as well as aseptic/clean clinical procedures for surgical procedures, wound dressing, and similar activities, to prevent infection.

7. Safe Injections and Sharps Injury Prevention

  • Prepare injections in a clean workspace with low risk of contamination from blood, body fluid, splashes, or sprays.
  • Perform hand hygiene before preparing medication and touching the patient.
  • Use a sterile, safety-engineered syringe; a sterile medication vial and diluent; and a sterile syringe and needle to withdraw and reconstitute medications — never leave a needle in the septum of a vial.
  • Avoid multi-dose vials, or if used, dedicate the vial for single-patient use; label it with the date opened and discard per manufacturer's instructions, when sterility is compromised, or after 28 days.
  • Clean the patient's skin with soap and water or disinfect with 60–70% alcohol before the procedure.
  • Provide a puncture-resistant sharps container at the point of care.
  • Do not re-cap, bend, break, manipulate, or manually remove the needle from the syringe.
  • Discard the sharps container when it is three-quarters full, seal it, and store it in a secure area.

8. Environmental Cleaning

Clean and disinfect patient care areas at least once a day, paying particular attention to frequently touched surfaces. Deal with spills of blood and body fluids/substances as soon as possible, in accordance with local protocols.

9. Handling and Transport of Linen

Handle soiled linen and waste carefully (with minimal manipulation) to prevent personal contamination and transfer to other patients. Remove heavily soiled material (e.g. feces) from linen — while wearing appropriate PPE — before placing it in the laundry bag. Store clean linen in a manner that protects it from environmental contaminants.

10. Safe Disposal of Waste (Including Sharps)

Treat waste contaminated with blood, body fluids, secretions, and excretions as hazardous infectious waste, in accordance with local regulations. Human tissue and laboratory waste directly associated with specimen processing is also treated as hazardous infectious waste. Health workers should minimize the amount of waste produced by the healthcare facility.

11. Decontamination and Reprocessing of Reusable Patient Care Items and Equipment

Reusable medical devices are devices that healthcare providers can reprocess and reuse on multiple patients (e.g. surgical forceps, endoscopes, stethoscopes). Health workers should handle equipment soiled with blood, body fluids, secretions, and excretions in a manner that prevents skin and mucous membrane exposure, contamination of clothing, and transfer of pathogens to other patients or the environment. Reusable equipment must be cleaned and disinfected, or sterilized, before use with another patient according to the manufacturer's instructions and national or international standards, and single-use devices must be discarded after each use.

Key Points / Quick Review

Infection Control & HAI Basics

  • Infection control = policies/procedures to control & minimize spread of infection in healthcare settings
  • HAI = infection not present or incubating at time of admission; includes staff occupational infections
  • WHO data: HAI rate 25% in developing countries, 5–15% in developed countries
  • Everyone at/visiting a healthcare facility shares responsibility for prevention

The Chain of Infection

  • Six links: Infectious Agent → Reservoir → Portal of Exit → Mode of Transmission → Portal of Entry → Susceptible Host
  • Breaking just ONE link stops the spread
  • Direct transmission = skin-to-skin/droplets; indirect = airborne, vehicleborne, or vectorborne

Common HAI Types & Organisms

  • CAUTI: E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Proteus
  • SSI: S. aureus (esp. MRSA), VRE, Candida
  • VAP: S. aureus (MRSA), Gram-negative bacilli
  • GI infection (pseudomembranous colitis): Clostridium difficile

Two Categories of Precautions

  • Standard precautions: used for ALL patients, in ALL settings, at ALL times
  • Transmission-based precautions: added on top of standard precautions, based on Contact, Droplet, or Airborne mode

11 Elements of Standard Precautions

  • Risk assessment, hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene, patient placement
  • PPE, aseptic technique, safe injections/sharps prevention
  • Environmental cleaning, linen handling, waste management, decontamination/reprocessing

Hand Hygiene

  • 5 Moments: before touching patient, before procedure, after procedure/fluid exposure, after touching patient, after touching surroundings
  • Handwash 40–60 sec; alcohol hand rub 20–30 sec
  • Gloves never replace hand hygiene

Personal Protective Equipment

  • Gloves: never reused between patients; sterile gloves for aseptic procedures
  • Gown + waterproof apron if splash risk
  • Respirators (N95/FFP2): fit test + seal check, for airborne particles/aerosol-generating procedures

Safe Injections & Sharps

  • Never leave a needle in a vial septum
  • Never re-cap, bend, or manually remove needles
  • Discard sharps container when three-quarters full

Waste, Linen & Cleaning

  • Clean/disinfect patient areas at least once daily
  • Handle soiled linen with minimal manipulation, wearing PPE
  • Treat blood/body-fluid-contaminated waste as hazardous infectious waste
